title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data sourcing: an AI music generation system was allegedly built using copyrighted recordings without authorization from the rights holders. This is a pre-deployment failure, meaning it occurred before any user ever typed a text prompt, during the data collection and model training phase. Catching it would have required a rights-clearance review of the training corpus before training began, not after the product reached millions of users.

The legal picture is unresolved and involves multiple separate parties. Universal Music Group settled its claims and entered a licensing arrangement. Warner Music Group also settled and announced a collaborative platform. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging use of more than 30,000 recordings, and a class action brought by independent artists survived a dismissal motion and was transferred to a new venue. A musicians' union lawsuit over the UMG deal is also pending.

None of the lawsuits cited here have produced a final verdict, and no court has yet made a binding finding that Udio's training constituted infringement. The settlements reflect negotiated resolutions, not judicial rulings on liability. What the training data actually contained, and on what legal basis it was or was not used, remains a matter of active litigation.

summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, resolving a lawsuit that accused the company of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. UMG's CEO stated the deal reflects the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technology and creating new revenue opportunities. Financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

The lawsuit had alleged that Udio improperly used popular songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to train its AI system, which generates original music from text prompts. This represents Udio's first major licensing agreement with a record label. The company, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its launch. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
